lines.text: The tax collector has nothing of all this. He looks not on
others but on himself alone: "God be merciful to me a
sinner!" He knows and confesses that in the presence of
God he can raise no claim and must cast himself utterly on
the divine mercy. He would like to enjoy some favour with
God: "God be merciful to me a sinner!" But he has com-
pletely surrendered that claimfulness which supposes that
by our own achievements we can acquire merit with God.
It is just this which is the fundamental sin: to presume by
one's own strength to assert a claim before God. In the
presence of God no man can be worth anything on the
ground of his own merit; none can boast before God. Such
boasting infringes the honour of God as Creator. "What have
you that you did not receive? If then you received it, why
do you boast as if it were not a gift?" (I Cor. 4: 7) In his
claimfulness man forgets that he is God's creature. And
from this point of view it is a matter of indifference whether
he speaks of God as does the Pharisee or whether he ceases to
speak of God. Both attitudes are sinful; both show man's
self-assertive claims in the face of God; this is sin and self-
deception.
The reason why so many people resist the idea of allowing
God to become the controlling reality in their lives, the
reason why they are averse to acceptance of the Christian
message, is that they feel it would mean surrendering man's
claim to be his own master. They prefer to live in self-
deception rather than by grace, to live by meritorious
achievements rather than by the free gift of God.
Even on the plane of human intercourse some people feel
it to be very difficult to accept gifts. Of course to receive the
gift of something which one particularly desires and then to
possess it freely as one's own-that is agreeable to all men.
But to receive a gift in the fullest sense means not simply to
receive the gift as an object merely, but to be indebted chiefly
to the kindness of the giver, with the result that one enters
into a relation of dependence on the giver. Naturally if this
means an outward dependence, an outward obligation, we
are justified in feeling the situation to be repugnant. But a
